WORLD ATLAS — A KINGDOM THAT CAN BE MISUSED

Irreverents • Expansion proposal, not approved canon • 22 November 2026

# Status and premise

This document converts the established world-design principles into a COHERENT PROPOSED GEOGRAPHY and level vocabulary. All proper names, location counts, region borders, culture details and specific rewards are proposals; they have NOT been chosen by the project owner. What is decided: a dense, interconnected, primarily 2D side-scrolling world; the routes between destinations are playable and secret-filled; new party members and copied abilities unlock new ways to read old places; difficult bosses are not universal choke points; dynamic stealth, mayhem and responses can occur in ordinary inhabited places.

Guiding feeling: “I thought this was the route to the market; how did I end up underneath the oldest arena in the kingdom?”

# World-scale organizing idea

A story-obsessed kingdom has spent centuries building ceremonial routes between supposedly important sites: palace, temples, halls, monuments, heroic battlegrounds. Underneath the official geography is a much more interesting network of maintenance tunnels, forgotten military passages, waterways, creature burrows, ancient mirrors, abandoned mines, rooftop crossings and contraband routes.

The official world has maps, plaques, monuments and histories. The real world has shortcuts, unintended connections and secrets. The protagonists care much more about the latter.

This supports a very simple level-design rule: every major region should have a public entrance, at least one discoverable non-obvious connection, and at least one return visit justified by an acquired character capability.

# Spatial topology

Don't build disconnected “level worlds” linked only by portals. Build a contiguous playable spine with branches and loops, supplemented by strange mirror-like transitions and shortcuts.

Working core loop:

ROYAL CROWNWARD ↔ LANTERNMARKET ↔ BRAMBLEWAKE WOODS ↔ SILTGLASS WATERWORKS ↔ CINDERWORKS ↔ THE OLD ARENA ↔ ROYAL CROWNWARD.

A hidden lower ring (“WHISPERWAYS”) links multiple locations through sewers, foundations, old tombs and ducts.

A vertical ring (“SKYRAIL HEIGHTS”) connects castle tower, city roofs, forest canopy, mountain cranes and a suspended observatory.

The HALL OF LEGENDS sits at an apparently dignified prominent site but has overlooked service tunnels and at least two alternate routes into its secured collections.

The MAIN QUEST sites exist within these regions and beyond them; do not lay them out as a single required chain.

# 01 — CROWNWARD: the royal capital and palace

Public identity: the ceremonial heart of civilization, painted as the beginning of every important story.

Playable spaces: approach road; markets; guardhouses; rooftops; palace balconies; royal audience; vault; kitchens; drainage system; prison; towers and archives.

Signature behavior: NPCs can be in awe, grateful, offended or terrified of the party, sometimes simultaneously. Royal guards respond to public trouble while private servants and courtiers pursue their routines.

Signature first scene: the king drones on about the apocalypse. The player notices the stained glass behind him, champion armor, the wizard's odd items, a strange door, the chained beast and a suspicious treasury.

Secret grammar: a draft behind the dais; ceiling chains connecting chandelier to service loft; a barred window over a courtyard; courtiers changing shifts; cracks concealing the old foundations.

Returning stronger: flyer reaches the weather vane; tiny hero enters air vents; strong grappler moves a hidden counterweight; animal speaker understands a palace beast; acquired electricity activates a long-dead lift.

Alarm expression: audience guards → armored castle watch → mounted or mechanized patrol → elite champion response.

Why visit repeatedly: palace is not a one-time plot stage. It keeps hosting heists, audiences, searches, ceremonies, new barriers and memorable clashes.

Note: exact crown, royal family, captive beast and intrigue remain open.

# 02 — LANTERNMARKET: the ordinary city nobody can keep ordinary

Public identity: trade town of workshops, inns, celebration squares, bank, stables and guild warehouses.

Playable spaces: cobbled street-level corridors, shop interiors, bell tower, hidden alleys, basement vaults, market roofs, canals, tavern with a very throwable furniture arrangement.

Signature behavior: traders prize safety; townsfolk love whoever drives away monsters but become furious about property loss and theft.

Secrets: a locksmith's shop has a passage into a forgotten counting house; the bell tower's mechanical guts hide an unusual item; a cart parked in a peculiar place conceals a drainage path.

Returning stronger: talk to the stable creatures; enter shop vents; commandeer freight carts; investigate a locked guild floor; use a copied cutting power on old shutters.

Alarm expression: shopkeepers and neighbors → local watch → guild security → armored response dispatched from the capital. Reinforcements arrive along visible routes where feasible.

Why revisit: shifting trust changes hospitality and commerce; the town has valuable targets worth visiting by stealth or force; its street is a natural site for escalating pursuits.

# 03 — BRAMBLEWAKE WOODS: the forest that contains more forest

Public identity: a picturesque woodland with an allegedly well-understood trail system.

Playable spaces: low trails, root caves, hollow trunks, canopy bridges, animal paths, abandoned timber camps, an impossible-looking stone door.

Visual rhythm: cheerful grass-and-tree platforms with quiet deep background. Secrets are subtle, not neon-marked.

Secrets: crawl through a trunk and emerge far below the trail; discover a canopy route toward the capital's upper ramparts; enter a creature-run enclave where a recruitable specialist lives.

Returning stronger: tiny character explores burrows; flyer reaches branches; strong character moves petrified roots; nature-speaker negotiates a path that combat would obscure.

Alarm expression: territorial wildlife, flock retaliation, forest guardians and escalating swarms, not copy-pasted police.

Why revisit: access expands dramatically through new roster abilities. A familiar forest can contain several previously unknown layers.

# 04 — SILTGLASS WATERWORKS: pipes, waterways and lost rooms

Public identity: the system that keeps city aqueducts and fountains running.

Playable spaces: pump station, sluices, bridges, partially flooded halls, small boats, drainage channels, underwater cave, ancient archive with unstable floors.

Special opportunities: redirect flow, freeze or drain water, trigger a pressure mechanism, ride a current, sneak through an exhaust shaft. Environmental systems create alternate routes.

Secrets: a submerged gallery remains intact behind a waterfall; an apparently useless valve lets players empty part of a dungeon; a slow-moving maintenance ferry passes a sealed wall.

Returning stronger: swimmer or water-capable character finds deeper route; ice power creates temporary crossings; heavy character shifts gate; small infiltrator fits narrow pipe.

Alarm expression: public utility guards, patrolling maintenance machines, territorial water creatures.

Why revisit: reconfiguring waterways alters how previously traversed rooms connect.

# 05 — CINDERWORKS: the industrial ridge

Public identity: foundries, mining lifts and the kingdom's proud machinery.

Playable spaces: mine mouth, smelter, giant gear galleries, rail depot, crane room, furnace bridges, foundry owner's fortified office, old war-machine garage.

Special opportunities: steal anything that can be driven, pull or sever chains, use lifting machines as weapons, blast through material and create extraordinary roadblock collisions.

Secrets: a hidden control room above a crane; a self-contained test arena; a furnace access shaft leading into an earlier region.

Returning stronger: electricity operates old lifts; heat opens a particular sealed channel; grappler moves machine counterweights; tiny character reaches maintenance panels; flying character skips missing catwalks.

Alarm expression: industrial watch → pursuit scooters → armored wagons → enormous mechanized suppression platform that players may commandeer.

Why revisit: the place of maximum spectacle also contains some of the best stealth opportunities: cutting power, using noise as cover, and disappearing beneath moving machinery.

# 06 — THE OLD ARENA: public glory, buried consequences

Public identity: a crumbling monument to legendary combat, where citizens boast of past champions.

Playable spaces: exterior plaza, stands, fighting pit, under-arena holding cells, gear shafts, tombs, memorial arches and sealed depths.

Signature situation: an angry pursuit may end here and accidentally awaken undead gladiators. The players and their pursuers may temporarily align against a common threat.

Secrets: a competitor's tunnel, a buried crown, a secret underground exit, a resident character in an abandoned training wing.

Returning stronger: flyer traverses ruined rigging; brute breaks arena wall; stealth character enters under-seat passage; copied light/fire/ice affects ancient mechanisms.

Alarm expression: crowd retaliation and the arena's dormant defenders; can become a wildly disproportionate battle without being a required boss arena.

Why revisit: arena becomes a venue for glory, escape routes and possible Hall-worthy last stands, not just one scripted tournament.

# 07 — SKYRAIL HEIGHTS: a second world above the first

Public identity: watchtowers, old suspension roads, wind-powered transports, proud couriers.

Playable spaces: tall buildings, flying transport docks, crane cables, cliffs, cloud platforms, observation posts and strange airborne ruins.

Secrets: a tiny aerial landing that connects to the Hall's roof; a hanging cargo cage that transports a party member across the world; hidden weather control that changes traversal.

Returning stronger: flyer or grappler bypasses ordinary roads; wind power enables gliding; vehicle specialist steals air transport; teammate keeps a fan running while another crosses.

Alarm expression: fast air patrols and flying machines, with opportunities for hijack or flight escapes.

Why revisit: world connectivity should be felt physically when the player looks down and recognizes the routes they used earlier.

# 08 — THE WHISPERWAYS: the underside of everything

Public identity: practically none. Official maps barely admit it exists.

Playable spaces: old sewers, forgotten shelters, maintenance corridors, hollow walls, buried libraries, creatures' homes and sealed passages between official regions.

Secrets: some entrances are disguised as mundane plumbing; others are reached only by going the “wrong way” after an apparent dead end.

Returning stronger: most new character capabilities can reopen an older shortcut. Players may find one route without realizing it bypasses a major enemy checkpoint.

Alarm expression: isolated searchers, territorial dwellers, ancient security systems or pursuing guards who cannot safely follow everywhere.

Why revisit: rediscoveries convert scattered worlds into a connected mental map.

# 09 — THE HALL OF LEGENDS: museum, sanctuary and terrible idea

Public identity: institution that immortalizes great deeds, irrespective of whether they were virtuous.

Playable spaces: entry hall, gallery corridors, pedestals with captured player moments, archive vault, roof, staff rooms, security barracks, hidden display wing.

A player's past epic infiltrations, last stands and escapes can be represented as frames, titles, participant lists and contextual stats. The Hall itself can be robbed, attacked and defended, and can commemorate its own ordeal.

Secrets: modest maintenance corridors, a dangerous uncurated wing and a forgotten transit path; these are proposals, not mandatory content.

Returning stronger: better thieves, stronger fighters and newly acquired powers change what can be attempted at the very place that tells the party's history.

Alarm expression: museum guards → curated defenders → heavyweight exhibit-security machines. Preserved records must remain accessible even after environmental damage.

# 10 — THE SEAL SITES: where the serious story is happening

Proposed role: multiple places related to a real civilization-threatening crisis, embedded in or reachable from ordinary regions. They can be visited accidentally, avoided, entered out of order or approached for entirely non-heroic reasons.

Don't build them as a mandatory linear seven-stage road. A player might steal a powerful enemy's tool, destroy an altar to open an exit, or rescue somebody without realizing they've altered the main quest.

Their precise lore is discussed in the Main Quest proposal; not settled.

# Geographic content rules for level designers

A. Each major area has ordinary life and at least one activity unrelated to the main quest.

B. Every major area can support quiet discovery, provocation/reaction, and some form of escape.

C. Each area has at least one visible “not yet” curiosity and at least one entirely unadvertised secret.

D. Each area's traversal web gains at least one meaningful shortcut or alternate route over time.

E. Each area includes at least one memorable object or machine that a player might covet, steal, break or misuse.

F. Never make all routes to the next region depend on defeating one high-difficulty boss.

G. An area should invite both pristine infiltration and spectacular catastrophe in the same architecture.

H. World art should feel as clear and relaxed as the earlier preferred Amazing Mirror-like pixel references, with intense effects reserved for genuine moments of impact.

# Questions for owner review

Which locations excite you, and which seem too familiar? Should the setting be primarily one kingdom, multiple rival kingdoms, or something less medieval? Do you want vehicles to feel mostly magical/mechanical or include recognizable modern cars and motorcycles? How much of the world should be aboveground vs concealed? Is the central kingdom a strong enough home base for the long-term game? None of these is answered by this proposal.
